purpose: Two-week Amazon Solutions Architect rehearsal: explain the customer decision, tradeoff, failure mode and validation before naming more services.
experience_boundary: Your OCI and Databricks work is actual experience only where supported by your resume and confirmed details. Every AWS architecture below is a hypothetical translation or practice design, not evidence you deployed it. Say: In my OCI work I did X; on AWS I would evaluate Y because Z. A completed lab is a lab, not production AWS experience.
answer_frame: Clarify the customer outcome, workload shape, existing estate and constraints.
State measurable requirements: throughput, p95/p99 latency, availability, RPO/RTO, compliance and budget.
Draw the simplest viable data flow; explain why each component earns its place.
Compare one credible alternative and make the cost, reliability and operational tradeoff explicit.
Walk through a failure, detection, recovery and validation experiment; agree the next customer step.

priorities.name: Must explain without notes
priorities.when: Days 1-7, then daily retrieval practice. Master these before expanding breadth.

priorities.name: Working fluency
priorities.when: Days 6-11. Tie these to a customer scenario and one failure drill.

priorities.name: Targeted awareness
priorities.when: Days 10-12, only after P0 is fluent. Deepen if the job description or recruiter emphasizes it.

lab_policy: Labs are optional and are not executed by this preparation site. Prefer the offline exercise if time or billing access is limited. Use a dedicated sandbox, MFA and temporary credentials. Estimate current regional charges first, use synthetic data and a short timer, and inspect every resource after cleanup. AWS Budgets alerts are not a hard spending cap; billing and notifications can lag. No lab requires NAT gateways, paid database instances, EKS clusters, provisioned concurrency, OpenSearch domains or live Bedrock calls.

ALB troubleshooting and HTTP response codes
API Gateway REST versus HTTP APIs

topics.name: VPC, subnets, routes, IGW and NAT
topics.decision: Trace DNS, route table, security controls and return traffic. A public subnet has an internet-gateway route; an IPv4 instance also needs a public address for direct internet access.
topics.tradeoff: Use public ingress with private application/data tiers. NAT supplies outbound IPv4 connectivity, with a cost and availability design to justify.
topics.failure: A private subnet does not automatically have internet access. Check routes, NAT connectivity, DNS and security rules separately.
topics.say: I would trace DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP separately, then use the request-path walkthrough to choose a read-only diagnostic before changing anything.
topics.probe: Can the private worker download a package, and what happens if its egress path fails?

topics.name: Security groups, NACLs and private endpoints
topics.decision: Security groups are stateful allow controls on associated resources; NACLs are stateless subnet controls with allow and deny rules.
topics.tradeoff: Use security groups as the main workload boundary; add subnet controls for a specific requirement. Endpoints solve service connectivity, not all authorization.
topics.failure: A restrictive NACL can block return traffic. A private endpoint policy can still deny a request allowed by a role.
topics.say: I would allow the application security group to reach the database port and test both the route and permissions.
topics.probe: Why can a TCP connection fail even when the destination security group allows it?

topics.name: IAM roles, least privilege and Organizations
topics.decision: Use temporary role credentials, workload identities and narrowly scoped actions/resources. Applicable explicit denies override allows; trust policy and permissions answer different questions.
topics.tradeoff: SCPs limit member-account principals but do not grant access or restrict management-account principals/service-linked roles. Identity, resource, key, boundary, session and organization policies can all matter.
topics.failure: Example: s3:GetObject is allowed by the role but explicitly denied by the bucket policy outside an approved endpoint. The applicable deny wins; assuming a role does not bypass it.
topics.say: I would identify the principal, action, resource and request conditions, then evaluate the applicable policies.
topics.probe: Why does an assumed role still receive AccessDenied?

topics.name: EC2, Lambda and ECS on Fargate
topics.decision: Use EC2 for host control, Lambda for suitable event-driven functions, ECS on Fargate for managed container processes.
topics.tradeoff: Compare startup latency, invocation/runtime constraints, sustained utilization, dependencies and team ownership. Serverless still needs scaling and cost controls.
topics.failure: Unbounded compute scaling can overload a database or downstream API. Set concurrency/backpressure and test realistic bursts.
topics.say: For this workload I would compare a function against a container using its execution shape and operational constraints.
topics.probe: What changes if the job becomes continuous or latency-sensitive?

topics.name: ALB, NLB, API Gateway and CloudFront
topics.decision: ALB fits HTTP application routing; NLB fits transport-layer load balancing. Discuss API management and edge caching as separate needs.
topics.tradeoff: Select the API type deliberately: REST APIs support usage plans/API keys, unlike HTTP APIs. API keys are not authentication; use a supported authorizer or IAM.
topics.failure: Healthy load balancer targets can still fail customer requests if a dependency is unhealthy; test meaningful health checks.
topics.say: I would first ask whether this is a web application, a managed public API or a TCP service.
topics.probe: Where does TLS terminate and which component owns authentication?

topics.name: S3, EBS and EFS
topics.decision: Choose S3 for objects, EBS for block storage attached to compute and EFS for shared file access. Start with the access protocol.
topics.tradeoff: Compare sharing, latency, durability/recovery, lifecycle and access cost. S3 is not a drop-in POSIX filesystem.
topics.failure: A volume or mounted path is not a backup strategy. Test restore and permissions rather than relying on the storage label.
topics.say: I would ask whether the application needs object APIs, a block device or shared file semantics.
topics.probe: How would you move an application that requires a shared filesystem?

topics.name: S3 access, consistency, lifecycle and recovery
topics.decision: S3 provides strong consistency for object PUT/DELETE and subsequent reads. Keep buckets private and grant only required access.
topics.tradeoff: Separate storage durability from versioning, retention and recovery needs. Lifecycle choices trade retrieval behavior and cost against access patterns.
topics.failure: A valid but unwanted overwrite or delete requires recovery controls; strong consistency does not undo application mistakes.
topics.say: I would validate access boundaries and rehearse restoring the required object version.
topics.probe: Does strong consistency remove the need for versioning or backups?

topics.name: RDS/Aurora versus DynamoDB
topics.decision: Use RDS/Aurora for joins and flexible relational queries; DynamoDB supports regional ACID transactions too, but needs designed key-based access patterns.
topics.tradeoff: Compare consistency, indexing, partition skew and connection management. DynamoDB tables/LSIs support optional strong reads; GSIs are eventually consistent.
topics.failure: A hot key or inefficient query can defeat capacity planning. Test skewed traffic and realistic queries.
topics.say: I would choose the data model from the reads, writes, transactions and consistency requirements.
topics.probe: What new access pattern would cause you to reconsider this choice?

topics.name: Multi-AZ, read replicas and backups
topics.decision: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance standby serves failover, not reads. Read replicas address read scaling; backups address recovery.
topics.tradeoff: Distinguish DB instance deployments from Multi-AZ DB clusters and Aurora. Replica lag and failover behavior depend on the chosen topology.
topics.failure: An application must reconnect after failover; a read replica may return stale data. Neither feature replaces tested backups.
topics.say: I would clarify whether the customer needs availability, read throughput or recovery before proposing replication.
topics.probe: Can we serve reports from the standby, and what changes with a Multi-AZ DB cluster?

topics.name: SQS, retries, DLQs and idempotency
topics.decision: Use SQS to buffer work: receive hides a message, and delete acknowledges success. FIFO orders within a message group and deduplicates sends within a 5-minute window.
topics.tradeoff: Bound retries with backoff/jitter, extend visibility for long processing, and monitor DLQs plus redrive. Commit database changes and an outbox event atomically to avoid a publish gap.
topics.failure: The worker can commit a side effect then crash before deletion. Use a durable idempotency strategy for business effects.
topics.say: I would make duplicate delivery safe and monitor queue age alongside the dead-letter queue.
topics.probe: What happens if a payment succeeds but the worker crashes before acknowledging?

topics.name: Availability, RPO/RTO and disaster recovery
topics.decision: Start with tolerable data loss (RPO) and restoration time (RTO). Multi-AZ addresses zonal resilience; regional DR is a separate decision.
topics.tradeoff: Compare backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and active/active against recovery objectives and complexity.
topics.failure: Replication can propagate corruption; failover also needs data, identity, routing and dependency readiness.
topics.say: I would agree the recovery objectives, then prove them with a measured restore or failover drill.
topics.probe: What fails during a regional outage, and how do you prevent split-brain writes?

topics.name: Unit economics, right-sizing and cost controls
topics.decision: Estimate cost per customer transaction or workload unit using measured demand, service usage and data movement.
topics.tradeoff: Reduce waste before committing spend. Compare managed-service labor savings with runtime, storage, request, logging and transfer costs.
topics.failure: A cheaper compute rate can be outweighed by idle capacity or transfer. A budget alert does not instantly stop spend.
topics.say: I would baseline usage and cost, make one change, and validate performance plus unit cost.
topics.probe: Which assumptions dominate the estimate and how will we validate them?

topics.name: KMS, Secrets Manager and encryption boundaries
topics.decision: KMS manages cryptographic keys; Secrets Manager handles secret storage/retrieval and rotation. Use TLS in transit plus the required at-rest controls.
topics.tradeoff: Compare managed versus customer-managed keys from audit, separation of duties and lifecycle requirements. Encryption is distinct from authorization.
topics.failure: A role may read a resource but lack decrypt permission; a rotated credential can break clients that never refresh it.
topics.say: I would trace both data access and key access and rehearse credential rotation with the application owner.
topics.probe: Why can an application read encrypted data yesterday but receive a decryption error today?

topics.name: SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis and Step Functions
topics.decision: SNS supports fanout; EventBridge routes events by rules; Kinesis retains a stream for consumers/replay; Step Functions models workflow coordination.
topics.tradeoff: Choose work queue, pub/sub, event routing, stream or orchestration from semantics. Persistence/replay features are configuration- and service-specific.
topics.failure: A routing service does not eliminate downstream retries or duplicates. Ordering is scoped, never assume global ordering.
topics.say: I would separate the need to distribute an event from the need to buffer work and coordinate a workflow.
topics.probe: Can independent consumers replay history, and who tracks a multi-step business process?

topics.name: CloudWatch, CloudTrail, Config and runbooks
topics.decision: CloudWatch supports operational telemetry; CloudTrail records account/API activity; Config tracks resource configuration/compliance.
topics.tradeoff: Use customer-facing SLOs plus dependency metrics. Audit logs and operational logs answer different questions.
topics.failure: High CPU alone does not identify the customer impact. Correlate request IDs, latency, errors and recent changes.
topics.say: I would start from the customer symptom, compare against the baseline and follow the failing dependency.
topics.probe: Which evidence tells you who changed a resource versus why requests are slow?

topics.name: Migration strategy, DMS and DataSync
topics.decision: Assess dependencies and choose a migration strategy before tools. Evaluate DMS for supported database migration/CDC and DataSync for supported data transfer. Verify discovery-tool availability: Application Discovery Service is closed to new customers; AWS identifies AWS Transform as a current discovery path.
topics.tradeoff: Rehosting can reduce initial change; replatforming/refactoring may improve operations but increases testing and delivery risk.
topics.failure: Reconcile and rehearse cutover with one write authority. Once the target accepts writes, rollback requires tested reverse replication or reconciliation; switching DNS back can lose those writes.
topics.say: I would propose a representative pilot with success criteria, cutover rehearsal and an explicit rollback trigger.
topics.probe: What if the source continues receiving writes during migration?

topics.name: Bedrock, RAG, evaluation and guardrails
topics.decision: For a knowledge assistant, evaluate retrieval-grounded generation with Bedrock and Knowledge Bases against the customer task.
topics.tradeoff: Evaluate retrieval quality, groundedness, latency and cost on a representative test set. RAG and fine-tuning solve different needs.
topics.failure: Retrieved content may carry prompt injection or stale data. Enforce retrieval filters server-side from trusted identity, prevent bypass, isolate answer caches by authorization, and check source-link permissions. Guardrails do not apply to retrieved references.
topics.say: I would build an evaluation set, test retrieval and citations, and define escalation for uncertain answers.
topics.probe: How will you prevent one tenant from retrieving another tenant's documents?

topics.name: GenAI data handling and shared responsibility
topics.decision: Inventory the exact model/API, retention mode, invocation logs and inference profile. Cross-Region inference can process prompts outside the source Region; do not promise all data remains in the customer account or Region.
topics.tradeoff: Application logs, knowledge stores, tool calls and external integrations have their own permissions and retention choices.
topics.failure: A secure model endpoint does not stop sensitive prompts being written to an application log or sent to an external tool.
topics.say: I would inventory where prompts, retrieved content, outputs and logs travel and apply the customer's data policy.
topics.probe: Which components can retain customer content and who can read it?

topics.name: CloudFront, WAF and protected origins
topics.decision: CloudFront distributes content through edge locations; WAF applies HTTP/HTTPS request rules to supported protected resources.
topics.tradeoff: Choose cache keys and freshness deliberately; evaluate WAF rules with observed traffic. Edge protection complements origin and application controls.
topics.failure: Caching personalized content with an unsafe cache key can disclose data. A public alternate origin path can bypass intended controls.
topics.say: I would define cacheable content and test isolation, freshness and the origin access path.
topics.probe: What would you cache, and how would you avoid returning one user's content to another?

topics.name: ElastiCache and cache-aside
topics.decision: Evaluate an in-memory cache for measured hot reads or suitable ephemeral data; retain a clear source of truth.
topics.tradeoff: Define TTL, invalidation, eviction and acceptable staleness. A cache adds operational and consistency decisions even when managed.
topics.failure: A cold cache or synchronized expiry can stampede the database. Use bounded concurrency and a controlled refill plan.
topics.say: I would prove that caching improves the hot path and test how the database behaves when the cache disappears.
topics.probe: Which reads may be stale, and what happens when the cache is empty?

topics.name: Glue, Athena, Redshift and data governance
topics.decision: Evaluate Glue for catalog/ETL, Athena for querying S3 data, and Redshift for warehouse analytics using the actual workload.
topics.tradeoff: Compare data freshness, query concurrency, file layout, performance and governance. Keep the AWS version of Databricks work explicitly hypothetical.
topics.failure: A successful ETL run can publish wrong data. Validate schemas, quality and reconciliation before downstream consumption.
topics.say: I would benchmark representative queries and establish data-quality gates before choosing the platform.
topics.probe: Which customer requirement favors a warehouse over ad hoc lake queries?

topics.name: Hybrid connectivity and network scale
topics.decision: Know the questions for VPN, Direct Connect, peering, Transit Gateway and private service access: bandwidth, resilience, routing and overlapping address space.
topics.tradeoff: Treat dedicated connectivity and encryption as separate requirements. Compare topology and operations before adding network hubs.
topics.failure: An apparently redundant design can share a failure dependency. Validate routes and the actual failover path.
topics.say: I would document connectivity assumptions and test a single-link failure with the networking team.
topics.probe: Which dependency remains common to both connectivity paths?

topics.name: ECS versus EKS
topics.decision: EKS provides managed Kubernetes; evaluate it when Kubernetes APIs, ecosystem or existing skills are a real requirement. ECS offers an AWS-native orchestration path.
topics.tradeoff: Compare team expertise, platform operations, portability needs and integration burden before choosing an orchestrator.
topics.failure: A managed control plane does not mean application health, networking, permissions and capacity operate themselves.
topics.say: I would ask what requires Kubernetes and who will own the platform before selecting EKS.
topics.probe: How does the customer benefit from Kubernetes enough to justify its operational model?

comparisons.title: Security group vs NACL
comparisons.answer: Stateful resource-level allow rules vs stateless subnet-level allow/deny rules.
comparisons.trap: A NACL needs return-path rules; adding an allow security group does not override a NACL deny.

comparisons.title: IGW vs NAT gateway
comparisons.answer: IGW is an internet routing component; a public NAT gateway enables outbound IPv4 from private workloads.
comparisons.trap: A public subnet route alone does not give every IPv4 resource internet connectivity.

comparisons.title: Gateway endpoint vs NAT
comparisons.answer: S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints provide service routes; NAT handles broader outbound internet paths.
comparisons.trap: A gateway endpoint is not generic internet access or a blanket authorization grant.

comparisons.title: Lambda vs Fargate
comparisons.answer: Event-driven functions vs container processes: compare execution shape, runtime needs and operations.
comparisons.trap: Serverless does not mean infinite concurrency or zero cost when idle in every configuration.

comparisons.title: ALB vs NLB
comparisons.answer: Choose application-layer HTTP routing vs transport-layer balancing from the protocol requirement.
comparisons.trap: A load balancer is not the same as an API-management or edge-cache product.

comparisons.title: S3 vs EFS vs EBS
comparisons.answer: Object APIs vs shared files vs block devices.
comparisons.trap: Do not choose storage only by capacity or treat S3 as POSIX.

comparisons.title: Multi-AZ vs read replica
comparisons.answer: For RDS DB instances, synchronous standby supports HA; read replicas support read scaling.
comparisons.trap: A Multi-AZ DB cluster has different read behavior; name the deployment type.

comparisons.title: Aurora/RDS vs DynamoDB
comparisons.answer: Relational query/transaction needs vs designed key-value/document access patterns.
comparisons.trap: NoSQL does not remove data modeling or automatically solve hot keys.

comparisons.title: SQS vs SNS
comparisons.answer: Buffered work for consumers vs pub/sub fanout; SNS to separate SQS queues can combine them.
comparisons.trap: One SQS queue with multiple consumers distributes work, not a copy to each application.

comparisons.title: Standard vs FIFO queues
comparisons.answer: Standard tolerates duplicates and relaxed order; FIFO adds scoped ordering and deduplication semantics.
comparisons.trap: FIFO does not make external side effects transactional; retries after consumer failure still need idempotency.

comparisons.title: EventBridge vs Kinesis
comparisons.answer: Event routing by rules vs a retained stream processed by independent consumers.
comparisons.trap: Ask about ordering, retention and replay rather than calling every event flow streaming.

comparisons.title: High availability vs DR vs backup
comparisons.answer: Survive a component/zonal failure vs recover from a larger disaster vs restore a recoverable data point.
comparisons.trap: Replication alone does not protect against propagated application corruption.

comparisons.title: CloudWatch vs CloudTrail vs Config
comparisons.answer: Operational telemetry vs account/API activity vs configuration/compliance state.
comparisons.trap: A log of who changed a setting is different from request tracing and application latency.

comparisons.title: RAG vs fine-tuning
comparisons.answer: Retrieve relevant knowledge at inference vs adjust model behavior using training examples.
comparisons.trap: RAG still requires authorization, document quality and evaluation; citations can be wrong.

comparisons.title: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store
comparisons.answer: Purpose-built secret lifecycle and rotation vs centralized named configuration, including encrypted SecureString values.
comparisons.trap: Encryption alone does not supply a rotation workflow. Choose from secret lifecycle and configuration needs.

comparisons.title: WAF vs security groups
comparisons.answer: HTTP request inspection/rules vs stateful network allow controls for associated resources.
comparisons.trap: WAF rules do not replace authentication, authorization, patched code or origin network boundaries.

walkthroughs.name: Customer web application
walkthroughs.customer: A retailer needs an application that handles promotions without losing orders.
discovery: What is peak traffic, acceptable checkout latency and the business impact of failure?
Which transactions require consistency, and what are the RPO/RTO targets?
What team operates it, what must remain on premises, and what is the budget?
flow: Browser to DNS/edge layer; use an ALB for HTTP application routing where appropriate.
Application containers on ECS/Fargate across AZs, with private data access and scoped workload roles.
Use relational storage for order transactions if the model requires it; publish asynchronous work through a reliable handoff to SQS.
walkthroughs.tradeoff: Compare containers with a serverless API. Add caches only for a measured read problem and define invalidation. A database outbox can help avoid a commit/publish gap.
walkthroughs.challenge: The database fails over during checkout: explain reconnects, bounded retries and an idempotent order request without charging twice.
walkthroughs.validation: Measure checkout success and tail latency during burst and failover tests; verify order reconciliation and recovery objectives.

walkthroughs.name: Customer data platform
walkthroughs.customer: A customer has batch files and growing analytics demand; relate this to Databricks only as a hypothetical AWS design.
discovery: What are volume, freshness, schema and data-quality expectations?
Which datasets contain sensitive fields, and who may query them?
Is this batch analytics, transaction processing or real-time decisioning?
flow: Land immutable source objects in private S3 storage with recovery and retention controls.
Evaluate Glue/Spark processing for transformations and a catalog/governance layer suited to the customer.
Evaluate Athena for ad hoc S3 queries or Redshift for a warehouse workload; choose from query concurrency and performance needs.
walkthroughs.tradeoff: A managed lake pattern and a warehouse have different operational and performance tradeoffs. Benchmark the representative queries rather than claiming one is always cheaper.
walkthroughs.challenge: A batch is delivered twice and late: show idempotent partition processing, quality gates and how consumers discover corrected data.
walkthroughs.validation: Replay a small synthetic dataset; compare row counts, quality checks, freshness and cost per successful pipeline run.

walkthroughs.name: Customer Oracle migration
walkthroughs.customer: A customer wants to reduce infrastructure management while preserving business continuity.
discovery: Which Oracle features, licensing obligations and application dependencies must remain compatible?
How much downtime and data loss are acceptable, and can the application change?
What makes rollback possible after the target starts accepting writes?
flow: Assess compatibility and select rehost, replatform or refactor for the workload.
Pilot a supported target and migration tool; evaluate DMS replication with validation where suitable.
Rehearse cutover: drain/coordinate writes, verify replication and reconciliation, switch the application, observe and make a deliberate rollback decision.
walkthroughs.tradeoff: Preserving the engine can reduce change; moving engines can require schema and application changes. Migration replication does not perform every conversion automatically.
walkthroughs.challenge: Replication lag rises before cutover: delay the switch, protect source write ownership and use agreed go/no-go criteria.
walkthroughs.validation: Prove representative transaction behavior, data reconciliation, cutover time and recovery in a rehearsal.

walkthroughs.name: Customer document assistant
walkthroughs.customer: A company wants answers from its internal documents with traceable evidence.
discovery: Who can see which documents, and is multi-tenant isolation required?
What are answer-quality, latency and cost goals, and when should it refuse or escalate?
Where may source content, prompts, embeddings and logs be stored?
flow: Authenticate the user; map identity to authorized document scopes before retrieval.
Store approved source documents, chunk/index with an evaluated retrieval pipeline or Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Invoke an approved model with retrieved context; validate output, show source evidence and record safe operational metrics.
walkthroughs.tradeoff: Compare a retrieval approach with a simpler keyword search before adding generation. Model selection follows measured quality, latency, data controls and cost.
walkthroughs.challenge: A retrieved document says to reveal secrets: treat it as untrusted data, maintain policy boundaries and test adversarial examples.
walkthroughs.validation: Evaluate held-out questions, unsupported answers, cross-tenant access attempts, stale documents and a budgeted latency/cost sample.

walkthroughs.name: Trace a slow or failing HTTPS request
walkthroughs.customer: A customer says the website is down for some users. Diagnose before proposing a replacement architecture.
discovery: Which URL, users, locations and time window fail? Is it DNS failure, timeout, certificate error, HTTP error or slow content?
What changed, which paths still work, and what is the customer impact? Compare a successful request and a failing one.
May we inspect sanitized client timings, request IDs, load-balancer access logs and application telemetry? Agree a safe rollback trigger.
flow: Resolve the name: browser/OS/resolver cache first; a recursive resolver asks authoritative DNS when needed. Use dig to inspect the returned name/IP and TTL. Route 53 is not an HTTP proxy.

Trace TCP, TLS, then HTTP for a normal HTTPS connection. HTTP/3 uses QUIC instead of TCP. Use curl -v or timing output to distinguish name resolution, connect, handshake and response time; validate certificate hostname, trust and expiry without disabling verification.

At CloudFront/ALB, inspect cache behavior, target health and request logs. A 502 can come from an upstream reset or invalid response; a 504 can be a connection/response timeout. Follow the request ID before blaming the database.

With authorized host access, use ss -lnt to check listeners, curl to test a local health endpoint, top/free to inspect CPU or memory, df -h and df -i for space/inodes, and journalctl for the service error window. Compare routes, SGs, NACL return ports, DNS and process state; command availability depends on the OS.

Correlate dependency latency, connection-pool saturation, throttling and recent deployments. Restore service using the smallest evidence-backed reversible change, then validate the original failing user path.
walkthroughs.tradeoff: Read-only diagnosis preserves evidence and avoids widening access blindly. Health checks must represent useful service readiness without cascading an optional dependency failure across all targets.
walkthroughs.challenge: DNS works and TLS validates, but the ALB returns 504 while the app process is running. Explain how you distinguish a blocked target path, a saturated worker pool and a slow downstream call.
walkthroughs.validation: State a hypothesis and a discriminating observation at every hop. Confirm customer success rate and tail latency after recovery, retain sanitized evidence, and explain why ping alone cannot prove HTTPS or application health.

labs.name: Packet-path and IAM tabletop
labs.cost_gate: Default is offline: no AWS charges. If inspecting an existing sandbox, use read-only access and create nothing.
steps: Draw public ingress, private compute and private database subnets; annotate request and response paths.
Remove a route, then a security-group rule, then an IAM allow; explain which symptom each produces.
Write the least-privilege actions/resources for a worker reading one bucket prefix and consuming one queue.
labs.offline: Use a local diagram and a policy JSON sketch. Explain explicit-deny and role-trust cases aloud; no account required.
cleanup: Discard any temporary local diagram containing account identifiers.
If you inspected a sandbox, sign out and verify you created no resources.

labs.name: Optional SQS receive/retry/delete
labs.cost_gate: Requests can incur charges. Check current SQS regional pricing and account billing first; use a sandbox and a few synthetic messages only.
steps: Create one standard queue with a short, deliberate visibility timeout; record its name and Region.
Send one synthetic message, receive without deleting, then wait for visibility expiry and receive again.
Delete with the latest receipt handle and explain why business side effects need durable idempotency.
labs.offline: Simulate a queue using a local list and draw the visible/in-flight/deleted timeline, including a crash after processing.
cleanup: Delete the queue and any manually created test queues or DLQs.
Check the selected Region for remaining resources; review billing again after usage is processed.

labs.name: Optional private S3 recovery rehearsal
labs.cost_gate: Storage, requests and versions can incur charges. Use tiny synthetic text files; check current regional charges and do not enable paid add-ons.
steps: Create one private test bucket with public access blocked; enable versioning for this rehearsal.
Upload a tiny text object, overwrite it, and verify you can retrieve the previous version using its version ID.
Explain IAM scope, a delete marker and why versioning is distinct from an immutable backup policy.
labs.offline: Create two local file versions and a restore manifest, then describe the S3 permissions and recovery steps on paper.
cleanup: Remove every object version and delete marker, then delete the bucket; ordinary object deletion is insufficient in a versioned bucket.
Delete any additional resources you created and inspect billing after usage is processed.

labs.name: Offline retrieval and GenAI evaluation
labs.cost_gate: Default is offline with no model API calls or cloud charges. Live Bedrock/vector-store exercises are outside this lab.
steps: Write five synthetic source paragraphs and ten questions, including unanswerable and unauthorized cases.
For each question choose allowed evidence and draft the expected answer or escalation; add one prompt-injection paragraph.
Score evidence relevance, unsupported claims, permission leakage and refusal quality; explain what you would measure in a future pilot.
labs.offline: The entire exercise uses local text and a spreadsheet or paper scorecard. No real customer documents or hosted model required.
cleanup: Delete synthetic test material when no longer useful.
Verify you created no cloud model, index or knowledge-base resources.
